mainTopic: A scholar's response to insult, the finger-count of the פייס and the meaning of פקיע, and the ramp murder that preceded the פייס
overview: The amud opens by finishing a statement: a תלמיד חכם who does not 'avenge and hold a grudge like a snake' is not a real scholar. The גמרא challenges this from 'לא תקום ולא תטור' and goes through several rounds. It concludes that the scholar may keep a personal hurt in his heart, but he must forgive once the offender comes to appease him. Next the גמרא turns to the משנה about the פייס (the lottery of fingers). A healthy כהן puts out one finger. A sick כהן may put out two, but they count as only one. Along the way it explains the word פקיע: a split-ended whip used to punish cheating כהנים, which is why אביי changed his mind about its meaning. Then a ברייתא tells of a כהן murdered during the race up the ramp, followed by רבי צדוק's tearful speech and the father's shocking concern for the knife's טהרה. The גמרא works out that the murder came first but was seen as a freak crime, while the broken leg showed the race itself was dangerous and led to the פייס. Finally, the גמרא asks whether ירושלים can bring an עגלה ערופה at all. It begins quoting a ברייתא of ten special laws of ירושלים, which continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: A scholar who does not avenge like a snake is not a scholar
steps.stepSummary: The end of רבי יוחנן's statement: a תלמיד חכם who does not avenge and hold a grudge like a snake is not a true תלמיד חכם.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Any Torah scholar] who does not take revenge and hold a grudge like a snake is not a Torah scholar.
steps.whatsHappening: This amud opens in the middle of a statement that began on the previous עמוד. It says a real תלמיד חכם must stand up for his honor and not just let insults go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a surprising claim, because the Torah seems to forbid revenge. The idea is that an insult to a scholar is an insult to the Torah, so he may not simply ignore it. The rest of the סוגיא tests this claim and narrows it down.

keyTerms.meaning: holds a grudge, keeps the hurt
like a snake (which bites and holds onto its anger)

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean a scholar may act cruelly or take actual revenge. As the סוגיא develops, it means he does not have to drop the matter until he is appeased.

phrases.english: who does not avenge and hold a grudge like a snake —
phrases.notes: This finishes the line from the previous עמוד, where רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק, started: 'Any תלמיד חכם...'

phrases.english: is not a Torah scholar.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁאֵינוֹ נוֹקֵם וְנוֹטֵר כְּנָחָשׁ אֵינוֹ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a statement begun on the previous עמוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם must stand up for his honor and not simply let an insult go.

steps.title: But the Torah forbids revenge and grudges
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the statement from the פסוק 'לא תקום ולא תטור'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'You shall not take revenge and you shall not hold a grudge'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how a scholar could be told to take revenge when the Torah clearly forbids it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The statement in step 1 seems to directly clash with an explicit איסור in ויקרא. The words of the פסוק, תקום and תטור, match the words of the statement, נוקם and נוטר, exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: but isn't it written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: But isn't it written: 'You shall not take revenge and you shall not hold a grudge'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the statement of step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The statement that a scholar should be נוקם ונוטר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah explicitly forbids נקימה and נטירה, so how can a scholar be required to do them?

steps.title: That verse is about money matters
steps.stepSummary: Answer: the איסור of לא תקום ולא תטור refers to money matters, not personal insults.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse is written about money matters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק speaks about property and lending, not about insults to a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This splits the subject into two areas. Revenge over money or favors is forbidden. A scholar responding to a personal insult is a different area. The next steps bring a ברייתא to show the פסוק really is about money.

phrases.english: That one is written regarding money matters,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק forbids all revenge, including over insults.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is about money and favors, so a scholar's response to an insult is not included.

steps.title: A ברייתא defines revenge: the sickle and the axe
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows the case of נקימה: refusing to lend because the other person refused to lend to you.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: What is revenge and what is a grudge? Revenge: One said to him, 'Lend me your sickle.' He said, 'No.' The next day the second one said to him, 'Lend me your axe.' He answered, 'I will not lend to you, just as you did not lend to me.' That is revenge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove its answer. The example of נקימה is about lending tools, which is a money matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נקימה means paying someone back in kind: you refused me, so I refuse you. Every example in the ברייתא involves objects and lending. This supports the claim that the פסוק is about money.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: אֵיזוֹ הִיא נְקִימָה וְאֵיזוֹ הִיא נְטִירָה?
phrases.english: As it was taught: What is revenge and what is a grudge?
Revenge — one said to him: Lend me your sickle,
he said to him: No.

phrases.aramaic: לְמָחָר אָמַר לוֹ הוּא: הַשְׁאִילֵנִי קַרְדּוּמְּךָ,
phrases.english: The next day he (the one who refused) said to him: Lend me your axe,
he said to him: I will not lend to you,
just as you did not lend to me —
that is revenge.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא אֵיזוֹ הִיא נְקִימָה וְאֵיזוֹ הִיא נְטִירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That לא תקום is about money matters.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא defining נקימה through a case of lending tools.

steps.title: A ברייתא defines a grudge: the axe and the robe
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: נטירה means lending, but reminding the other person that he refused you.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is a grudge? One said to him, 'Lend me your axe.' He said, 'No.' The next day the second one said to him, 'Lend me your robe.' He answered, 'Here it is. I am not like you, who did not lend to me.' That is a grudge.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and defines נטירה, again through a lending case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נטירה you do the favor, but you keep the hurt and show it with a jab like 'I'm not like you.' Even this softer behavior is forbidden. Since this example is also about lending, the proof that the פסוק is about money is complete.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the two. נקימה means you refuse in return. נטירה means you agree but rub it in. Both are forbidden.

phrases.english: And what is a grudge?
One said to him: Lend me your axe,
he said to him: No.
The next day he said to him: Lend me your robe!
He said to him: Here it is,
I am not like you, who did not lend to me.
That is a grudge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That לא תטור is also about money matters.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same ברייתא's definition of נטירה through lending a robe.
steps.whyThisMatters: These two definitions are the classic halachic definitions of נקימה and נטירה used across halachic literature.

steps.title: But we praise those who stay silent when insulted
steps.stepSummary: Challenge: a ברייתא praises people who are insulted and do not respond. This shows that personal hurt should also be forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: And personal pain is not included? But it was taught: Those who are insulted but do not insult back, who hear their shame and do not answer, who act out of love and are happy in suffering, about them the verse says: 'And those who love Him are like the sun going out in its strength'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that only money matters are included. A ברייתא praises people who let personal insults go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ideal person swallows insults silently, then letting go of personal hurt is also expected. This seems to undo the answer of step 3. It also clashes with the claim that a scholar should be like a snake.

keyTerms.meaning: personal pain, a hurt to the person himself
but wasn't it taught? (challenge from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: And personal pain is not included?
But wasn't it taught:
Those who are insulted but do not insult,
who hear their shame and do not answer,
who act out of love and are happy in suffering,
about them the verse says:
'And those who love Him are like the sun going out in its strength'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the money-only answer of step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that only money matters are covered, so a scholar may respond to personal insult.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא praises silent acceptance of personal insult, so personal hurt must also be let go.

steps.title: He may keep it in his heart
steps.stepSummary: Answer: the scholar does not act on the insult or mention it, but he may keep it in his heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Actually, it means that he keeps it in his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes its answer. The scholar's 'snake-like' quality only means he holds the hurt inside without acting on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the גמרא agrees that personal insults are also covered by the ideal of not answering back. What is left for the scholar is only that he does not erase the hurt from his heart. Silence on the outside, as the ברייתא praises, fits with remembering on the inside.

keyTerms.meaning: he holds it in his heart

phrases.english: Actually, it means he keeps it in his heart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 by redefining what the scholar's 'revenge' means.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the scope of the original statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The scholar may actively respond to personal insults.
steps.terutzMaskana: He does not respond outwardly. He only keeps the hurt in his heart.

steps.title: But רבא says letting go earns forgiveness
steps.stepSummary: Challenge from רבא: whoever passes over his grievances is forgiven for all his sins. So even keeping it in the heart seems wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבא say: Whoever lets go of his grievances, they let go of all his sins for him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. רבא praises completely letting go, which seems to rule out even holding it in your heart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 allowed the scholar to keep the hurt inside. רבא's statement suggests the ideal is to drop it entirely, and Heaven rewards that with forgiveness. So why should a scholar hold on to anything?

keyTerms.meaning: but didn't [so-and-so] say? (challenge from a statement)
one who passes over his grievances (does not insist on payback)

phrases.english: But didn't רבא say:
Whoever passes over his grievances —
they pass over all his sins for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רָבָא כׇּל הַמַּעֲבִיר עַל מִדּוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permission to keep the hurt in his heart.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא praises full forgiveness, so holding on even internally seems improper.

steps.title: Forgive when he comes to appease you
steps.stepSummary: Final answer: רבא is talking about a case where the offender seeks to appease him, and then he must accept.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is when they appease him and he lets himself be appeased.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the conflict. When the offender apologizes, the scholar must let it go. Until then, he may keep it in his heart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ideas are now true in different situations. רבא's praise applies once someone tries to make peace, and then the scholar must forgive. Without an apology, the scholar may hold on to it for the honor of Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: and he allows himself to be appeased

steps.whatToRemember: A תלמיד חכם may not take revenge or rub in an insult, and לא תקום ולא תטור applies fully to money matters. For a personal insult he may keep it in his heart, but once the offender comes to appease him, he must forgive.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shapes the practical הלכה that one must accept a sincere apology and not stay stubborn. It also leaves room for a scholar to protect the honor of Torah.

phrases.english: When they appease him, and he lets himself be appeased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 and closes the סוגיא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא requires dropping every grievance immediately.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא speaks of a case where the offender seeks to appease him. Without an apology, the scholar may keep the hurt in his heart.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: one or two fingers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line in the משנה that the כהנים may put out one or two fingers for the פייס.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And what do they stick out? One or two fingers, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה about the lottery. This quote sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פייס, each כהן sticks out a finger and the officer counts the fingers to pick who does the עבודה. The משנה lets a כהן stick out one finger or two. The גמרא will now look closely at that wording.

keyTerms.meaning: they stick out (fingers, for the count)
the lottery among the כהנים to decide who does a Temple job
'etc.' The quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: And what do they stick out?
One or two fingers, etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה continues: but they do not stick out a thumb in the מקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה הֵן מוֹצִיאִין — אַחַת אוֹ שְׁתַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It goes back to the משנה about the פייס and leaves behind the earlier discussion of נטירה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן may stick out one or two fingers for the lottery count.

steps.title: If two fingers are allowed, why mention one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה bothers to say 'one' if even two fingers are allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that they may stick out two fingers, do we even need to be told they may stick out one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the משנה. If two fingers are allowed, then one finger is obviously allowed, so why say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes 'one or two' are two options for the same person. If so, saying 'two' already covers 'one,' and the extra word seems wasted. The answer will have to show that 'one' and 'two' apply to different people.

keyTerms.meaning: now that (if this bigger case is true)
is it necessary? (it should be obvious)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question about the הלכה. Everyone agrees one finger is fine. The question is only about why the משנה uses extra words.

phrases.english: Now that they stick out two fingers,
is it necessary to say one?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It attacks the wording of the משנה just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'one or two' in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a הַשְׁתָּא ... מִבַּעְיָא argument. If the bigger case (two) is allowed, the smaller case (one) is obvious, so mentioning it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: One finger for a healthy כהן, two for a sick one
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers that 'one' refers to a healthy כהן and 'two' refers to a sick כהן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: This is not difficult. Here (one finger) is about a healthy person. There (two fingers) is about a sick person.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question by splitting the משנה into two different people. A healthy כהן puts out one finger, and a sick כהן may put out two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed 'one or two' was a free choice for everyone. רב חסדא says it is not a choice. A healthy כהן must use one finger, while a sick כהן, who has trouble holding out a single finger by itself, may use two. So neither word is extra.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (the two parts deal with different cases)
here ... there (each part refers to a different case)

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: It is not difficult:
Here, with a healthy person; there, with a sick person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא, לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בְּבָרִיא, כָּאן בְּחוֹלֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the question about why the משנה says 'one.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא). Each number in the משנה refers to a different kind of person.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One or two' was a free choice for every כהן, so 'one' looked unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'One' is the rule for a healthy כהן. 'Two' is an allowance for a sick כהן.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא matches רב חסדא: a healthy כהן puts out one finger and a sick כהן may put out two, but the two count only as one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it was taught in a ברייתא: They stick out one finger, but not two. When is this said? About a healthy person. But a sick person may stick out even two. And the sick ones who sit by themselves stick out two, but they are counted as only one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רב חסדא said. It also adds a new detail: a sick כהן's two fingers count as just one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא confirms the healthy and sick split. Its last line adds something new. The sick כהנים, who sit apart from the others, put out two fingers, but the officer counts that hand as one. This stops the extra finger from changing who wins the lottery.

keyTerms.meaning: in what case is this said? (this limits the rule)
those sitting by themselves (here, the sick כהנים)

steps.confusionAlert: Usually וְהָתַנְיָא introduces a challenge. Here it means 'and so it was taught,' because the ברייתא supports רב חסדא.

phrases.english: And so it was taught: One finger, they stick out;
two, they do not stick out.
In what case is this said? With a healthy person;
but a sick person may stick out even two.
And those sitting by themselves stick out two,
phrases.notes: This refers to the sick כהנים, who sit or lie apart from the others.

phrases.english: but they are counted only as one.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: אַחַת — מוֹצִיאִין, שְׁתַּיִם — אֵין מוֹצִיאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It supports רב חסדא's answer with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's split between a healthy כהן and a sick כהן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that says this split directly and adds that the sick כהן's two fingers count as one.
steps.whyThisMatters: The new rule, that two fingers count as only one, is what the next challenge will attack.

steps.title: A ברייתא suggests the middle finger is counted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the rule that two fingers count as one, using a ברייתא that says an extra middle finger 'is counted.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they really counted as only one? But it was taught: They do not stick out the middle finger or the thumb, because of cheaters. But if he did stick out the middle finger, it is counted for him. If he stuck out the thumb, it is not counted, and not only that, he is hit by the officer with the פקיע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that two fingers count as one. Another ברייתא says that if a כהן puts out his middle finger, 'it is counted,' which sounds like it counts as an extra finger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second ברייתא bans an extra middle finger or thumb, because someone could add a finger to make the count land on himself. Still, it says an extra middle finger 'is counted,' since it sits right next to the pointer finger and clearly belongs to the same hand. That sounds like both fingers count, which goes against 'counted only as one.'

keyTerms.meaning: the third finger, meaning the middle finger
cheaters (who try to make the lottery fall on themselves)
a whip or strap used by the officer

phrases.english: And are they really counted for him as only one?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: אֵין מוֹצִיאִין לֹא שָׁלִישׁ וְלֹא גּוּדָל
phrases.english: But it was taught: They do not stick out the middle finger or the thumb
because of the cheaters.
But if he stuck out the middle finger, it is counted for him;
the thumb is not counted for him,
and not only that, but he is struck
by the officer with the strap.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מוֹנִין לוֹ אֶלָּא אַחַת? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It attacks the last line of the supporting ברייתא, that two fingers count as only one.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a כהן's two fingers are counted as only one.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second ברייתא says an extra middle finger 'is counted for him.' That seems to mean it counts as an additional finger, against the rule that two count as one.

steps.title: 'Counted' means counted as one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'it is counted for him' also means the two fingers count as just one.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'it is counted for him' mean? It also means: as one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by explaining what 'counted' means. The middle finger does not add to the count. The hand is still counted as one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second ברייתא only means that the כהן is not thrown out of the lottery for adding a middle finger. Unlike the thumb, it does not cancel his entry. His two fingers still count as one, so the two ברייתות agree.

keyTerms.meaning: what does it mean? (introduces an explanation)

steps.whatToRemember: In the פייס, a healthy כהן puts out one finger. A sick כהן may put out two, but they count as one. An extra middle finger still counts as one, while a thumb is not counted at all and earns a punishment.

phrases.english: What does 'it is counted for him' mean? Also as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the challenge by reading the second ברייתא in a way that fits the first.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'It is counted for him' means each finger counts separately.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'It is counted for him' means the hand stays in the lottery and is counted as one, like a sick כהן's two fingers.

steps.title: What is a פקיע?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word פקיע means, and רב answers that it is a מדרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a פקיע? רב said: it is a מדרא.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from before said a cheating כהן gets struck by 'the one in charge of the פקיע.' Now the גמרא stops to ask what that word means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack. It is a simple word question. רב replaces the unclear word פקיע with another word, מדרא. But that word is also unclear, so the next step will have to explain it too.

keyTerms.meaning: An unclear word from the ברייתא; the גמרא is trying to define it
רב's explanation of פקיע; itself needs explaining
What is? (the opening of a definition question)

phrases.english: What is a pakia?
Rav said: It is a madra.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to a word in the ברייתא quoted in step 14 (the one in charge of the פקיע) and asks what it means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word פקיע.

steps.title: What is a מדרא? An Arab whip with a split end
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what מדרא means, and רב פפא explains that it is an Arab whip whose end is split into strands.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a מדרא? רב פפא said: a whip used by Arabs, whose end is split.
steps.whatsHappening: רב's word מדרא was also unclear, so the גמרא asks again. רב פפא gives a clear picture: a split-ended whip.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the meaning is finally clear. The פקיע was a whip used to punish כהנים in the מקדש. So 'the one in charge of the פקיע' was the man in charge of giving lashes.

phrases.english: What is a madra?
Rav Pappa said: An Arab whip
whose end is split.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the word that רב used in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of רב's word מדרא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב פפא: a split-ended Arab whip.
steps.whatToRemember: פקיע = a split-ended whip used to punish כהנים in the מקדש.

steps.title: אביי's first guess: פקיע means wicks
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that at first he thought בן ביבאי, who was 'in charge of the פקיע,' was in charge of making wicks. He based this on a משנה that uses the verb מפקיעין for tearing old priestly clothes into wicks.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: At first I would say that when we learned 'בן ביבאי was in charge of the פקיע,' it meant wicks. As we learned: from the worn-out trousers and belts of the כהנים they would tear strips, and with them they would light.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tells us how he used to understand the word פקיע. He thought it meant wicks. This sets up his change of mind in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A different משנה lists בן ביבאי as the one 'in charge of the פקיע.' אביי connected the word to another משנה where מפקיעין means 'they tore' old priestly clothes to make wicks for the lamps. So he assumed פקיע meant wicks.

keyTerms.meaning: At first I would say (a view I later dropped)
A Temple official listed in a משנה as in charge of the פקיע

phrases.english: Abaye said: At first I would say
regarding that which we learned in a mishna:
Ben Beivai was in charge of the pakia,
I would say it means wicks.
As we learned in a mishna:
From the worn-out trousers of the priests and from their belts,
from them they would tear strips,
phrases.notes: This verb shares a root with פקיע, which is why אביי linked the two.

phrases.english: and with them they would light the lamps.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the definition of פקיע. אביי tells how he once read the same word another way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי's first view: in the משנה about בן ביבאי, פקיע means wicks, based on the verb מפקיעין in another משנה.

steps.title: אביי changes his mind: פקיע means lashes
steps.stepSummary: After hearing the ברייתא that a כהן is flogged by 'the one in charge of the פקיע,' אביי realizes that פקיע means lashes, not wicks.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once I heard what is taught in the ברייתא, 'and moreover, he is flogged by the one in charge of the פקיע,' I now say: what is פקיע? Lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי drops his earlier view. The ברייתא shows that the official in charge of the פקיע gives lashes, so the word must mean a whip or lashes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wicks do not fit with the word 'flogged' (לוקה). Since the ברייתא links the פקיע official to giving lashes, בן ביבאי must have been in charge of punishment in the מקדש. This matches רב and רב פפא's whip explanation.
steps.whatToRemember: בן ביבאי was in charge of lashes in the מקדש, not wicks. The ברייתא's wording proves it.

phrases.english: Once I heard that which is taught in a baraita:
And moreover, he is flogged
by the one in charge of the pakia,
I now say: What is a pakia? Lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's own first reading from step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only אביי's earlier reading of פקיע as wicks.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא ties the פקיע official to flogging, so 'wicks' does not fit the context.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: two כהנים racing up the ramp
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line of the משנה about two כהנים who were tied as they ran up the ramp.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: there was an incident where both were equal as they were running and going up the ramp.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. It quotes the story of the ramp race to set up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, one כהן pushed the other, who fell and broke his leg. This led to the system of the פייס (the lottery). Here the quote is only a heading, so the גמרא can bring a parallel source.

keyTerms.meaning: The ramp leading up to the מזבח

phrases.english: An incident occurred where both of them were equal
as they were running and ascending the ramp.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁהָיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶן שָׁוִין וְרָצִין וְעוֹלִין בַּכֶּבֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. The word discussion is finished, and the גמרא returns to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the משנה's story of the tied race up the ramp as a heading.

steps.title: The ברייתא's version: one כהן stabbed the other
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells of two כהנים racing up the ramp. When one got ahead into the four אמות first, the other took a knife and stabbed him in the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: there was an incident with two כהנים who were equal as they ran up the ramp. One of them got into the four אמות ahead of his friend. The other took a knife and stabbed him in the heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a much worse ramp story than the one in the משנה. Here the race ended in murder, not a broken leg.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The race was to reach within four אמות of the מזבח first and win the job of removing the ashes. In the משנה, the result was an injury. In this ברייתא, the losing כהן killed the winner. The next steps continue the ברייתא with the public reaction. Step 26 then asks how the two stories fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, the finish line near the מזבח

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different, more violent story than the one in the משנה (a broken leg). Do not mix the two together.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: An incident with two priests
who were both equal
as they were running and ascending the ramp.
One of them got ahead
into the four cubits before his colleague,
and the other took a knife and stabbed him in his heart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ברייתא to the משנה line quoted in step 20, with a harsher ending.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In one ramp race, the losing כהן murdered the winner with a knife.

steps.title: רבי צדוק's speech about עגלה ערופה and the people's tears
steps.stepSummary: רבי צדוק stands on the steps of the אולם and asks the people: under the עגלה ערופה law, who must bring the calf for this killing, the city or the Temple courtyards? All the people burst into tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי צדוק stood on the steps of the אולם and said: Listen, our brothers, house of Israel! The פסוק says, 'If a slain person is found in the land... then your elders and your judges shall go out.' As for us, on whom does it fall to bring the עגלה ערופה? On the city, or on the courtyards? All the people burst out crying.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי צדוק responds to the murder with a sharp public speech based on the law of עגלה ערופה. The people react by weeping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עגלה ערופה is brought when a body is found and the killer is unknown. Here the killer was known and the murder happened inside the מקדש, so the law does not really apply. רבי צדוק uses it as a pointed rebuke: 'Who is responsible for this blood, the city or the מקדש?' The question shows how shameful the event was, and that is why everyone cried.

keyTerms.meaning: The steps of the entrance hall of the היכל
The calf whose neck is broken, brought for an unsolved murder

steps.whyThisMatters: The speech shows how far competition over מקדש service had gone. The גמרא will soon ask how this murder relates to the פייס. It concludes that the murder was seen as a freak crime, and only the broken leg led to the פייס (step 30).

phrases.aramaic: עָמַד רַבִּי צָדוֹק עַל מַעֲלוֹת הָאוּלָם,
phrases.english: Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps of the Entrance Hall,
and said: Our brothers, house of Israel, listen!
The verse states:
"If one be found slain in the land...
phrases.notes: דברים כא:א-ב; the middle of the verse is left out.

phrases.english: then your elders and your judges shall go out."

phrases.aramaic: אָנוּ, עַל מִי לְהָבִיא עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה?
phrases.english: As for us, upon whom is it to bring the heifer whose neck is broken?
Upon the city, or upon the Temple courtyards?
All the people burst out in weeping.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָמַד רַבִּי צָדוֹק עַל מַעֲלוֹת הָאוּלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with the public reaction to the murder.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי צדוק rebukes the people with a pointed עגלה ערופה question, and all the people weep.

steps.title: The father finds his son still convulsing and worries about the knife
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the stabbed boy's father arrives and says the knife is still טהור, because his son has not yet died.
steps.simpleTranslation: The boy's father came and found him still convulsing. He said: 'May he be your atonement. My son is still convulsing, so the knife has not become impure.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps telling the story of the murdered כהן. It now describes how the boy's father reacted when he arrived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a person dies, he makes the objects touching him טמא through טומאת מת. Since the boy was still alive, the knife in his body was still טהור. The father hurries to point this out, so the knife can be pulled out and used again for קדשים.

keyTerms.meaning: Convulsing, twitching — still alive but dying
Your atonement (let him atone for you)

steps.confusionAlert: The father's concern for the knife's טהרה is not presented as a good thing. The ברייתא tells this story to criticize the people's twisted priorities, as the next line says.

phrases.english: The father of the boy came
and found him while he was still convulsing.
He said: Let him be your atonement,
phrases.notes: He uses the common phrase of mourning and atonement.

phrases.english: and my son is still convulsing,
so the knife has not become impure.
phrases.notes: A living person does not transmit טומאת מת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's story right after the people burst into tears at רבי צדוק's words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The father's first concern is that the knife is still טהור, because his son has not yet died.

steps.title: The lesson: purity of vessels mattered more to them than murder
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states the moral of the story: in those days, טהרת כלים bothered people more than שפיכות דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches you that the purity of vessels was harder for them than the shedding of blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא steps back from the story and tells us its point. People cared more about keeping vessels טהור than about a person being murdered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father's reaction is the proof of a broken value system. He was more upset about a vessel possibly becoming טמא than about his son's killing. The ברייתא presents this as a sharp criticism of that generation.

keyTerms.meaning: To teach you (introduces the lesson of a story)

phrases.english: To teach you that it was harder for them
the purity of vessels
more than the shedding of blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the moral from the father's reaction in the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: That generation cared more about טהרת כלים than about שפיכות דמים.

steps.title: A verse about מנשה shows the same disregard for blood
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא supports its lesson with a פסוק saying that מנשה filled ירושלים with innocent blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: And similarly it says: 'And also מנשה shed very much innocent blood, until he filled ירושלים from one end to the other.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק to show that this kind of disregard for human life had happened in ירושלים before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the days of מנשה, killing became so common that the city was 'filled' with blood. The ברייתא connects this to its own time to show the same moral failure.

keyTerms.meaning: From end to end (literally 'mouth to mouth')

phrases.english: And similarly it says:
"And also Manasseh shed innocent blood, very much,
until he filled Jerusalem
from one end to the other."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a scriptural parallel for the lesson in step 24.
steps.raayaObject: That bloodshed was treated lightly in ירושלים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in מלכים ב about מנשה filling ירושלים with innocent blood.

steps.title: Which incident happened first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which came first: the broken leg in the משנה or the murder in the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which incident came first?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now compares the two stories it has heard. This question sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the פייס was made because of a broken leg. The ברייתא tells of a murder during the race. The גמרא wants to know the order, because that tells us why the פייס was made.

phrases.english: Which incident came first?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתא's story and asks how it fits with the משנה's story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The order of the two incidents: the broken leg and the murder.

steps.title: The murder could not have come first, or the lottery would have come then
steps.stepSummary: If the murder came first, why make a פייס only after a broken leg and not after a killing?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the murder came first: if after a murder they did not make a lottery, would they make one after a broken leg?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests one possible answer: that the murder came first. It shows that this answer seems impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A murder is far worse than a broken leg. If the חכמים did not change the system after a killing, it makes no sense that they would change it after a smaller injury.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a possibility to be tested)
Now, if — introduces a 'how much more so' argument
The lottery (פייס) for assigning Temple jobs

phrases.english: If you say the bloodshed came first,
now, for bloodshed
they did not institute a lottery,
for a broken leg they instituted one?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests and rejects the first possible answer to the question in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possibility that the murder happened before the broken leg.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is a קל וחומר: a lesser injury would not bring a reform that a greater tragedy did not bring.

steps.title: So the broken leg must have come first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes for now that the broken leg happened first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the broken leg came first.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the murder-first answer was rejected, the גמרא suggests the opposite order: the broken leg came first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this order, the משנה makes sense: the broken leg led to the פייס. This answer is only temporary, and the next step will challenge it.

phrases.english: Rather, the broken-leg incident came first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected order with the opposite one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The broken leg came first, and it led to the פייס.

steps.title: If there was already a lottery, why were they still racing?
steps.stepSummary: After the פייס was made, there was no race, so how could the murder happen while running to the four אמות?
steps.simpleTranslation: But once they instituted the lottery, what were they doing at the four cubits?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave. If the broken leg came first and the פייס was made right after it, the later murder story makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The murder happened during a race to reach the four אמות first. That race only existed before the פייס. So the murder must have happened before the פייס was made.

keyTerms.meaning: The four cubits near the מזבח — the finish line of the race

phrases.english: And since they had instituted the lottery,
what business did they have with the four cubits?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the broken leg came first.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: After the פייס there was no race, but the murder happened during a race. So the murder must have come before the פייס.

steps.title: The murder came first but was seen as a freak event
steps.stepSummary: The murder did come first, but the חכמים thought it was a one-time accident. Only when the broken leg showed that even ordinary racing is dangerous did they make the פייס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really the bloodshed came first. At first they thought it was just a chance event. Once they saw that even on its own the race leads to danger, the רבנן instituted a lottery.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the first order (murder first). It explains why that order still makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A murder is a deliberate crime, so the חכמים did not see it as a problem built into the race. A broken leg from pushing showed that the race itself, without any evil intent, puts people in danger. That is the kind of risk that calls for a change in the system, so they made the פייס.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (returns to an earlier position)

steps.whatToRemember: The murder came first but was treated as a rare crime. The broken leg showed that the race itself was dangerous, and that is why the פייס was made.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a תקנה is made to address a risk built into a system, not a one-time event.

phrases.english: Rather, actually the bloodshed came first,
and at first they thought
it was merely a chance occurrence.
Once they saw that even on its own
they come to danger —
the Rabbis instituted the lottery.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 29 and removes the problem raised in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of motive: explains why the bigger tragedy did not lead to a reform.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A murder should surely have led to the פייס at once.
steps.terutzMaskana: The murder was seen as a freak crime. The broken leg showed a built-in danger, so it led to the פייס.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The order was: murder, then broken leg, then the פייס.

steps.title: Quoting רבי צדוק's עגלה ערופה question again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי צדוק's speech again so it can examine it in detail.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי צדוק stood on the steps of the אולם and said: 'Our brothers, house of Israel, listen! The verse says: If a slain person is found in the land. As for us, for whom do we bring the calf? For the city, or for the courtyards?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא and repeats רבי צדוק's words. It is setting up a question about them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real repetition. Before, the line was part of the story. Now the גמרא quotes it to examine its halachic assumption, namely that ירושלים might bring an עגלה ערופה.

keyTerms.meaning: The steps of the Temple's entrance hall

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new story. It is the same words of רבי צדוק from step 22, quoted again so the גמרא can ask about them.

phrases.aramaic: עָמַד רַבִּי צָדוֹק עַל מַעֲלוֹת הָאוּלָם
phrases.english: Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps of the Entrance Hall
and said: Our brothers, house of Israel, hear!
Behold, it says:
"If a slain person is found in the land,"
we — on whose behalf must we bring?
On behalf of the city, or on behalf of the courtyards?

steps.triggerLanguage: עָמַד רַבִּי צָדוֹק עַל מַעֲלוֹת הָאוּלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the order-of-events discussion to the ברייתא's story, to analyze רבי צדוק's words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי צדוק asks whether the city or the עזרות must bring the עגלה ערופה for this killing.

steps.title: Can ירושלים even bring an עגלה ערופה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי צדוק's question: is ירושלים subject to עגלה ערופה at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: But is ירושלים subject to bringing an עגלה ערופה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the basic assumption behind רבי צדוק's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי צדוק spoke as if ירושלים or the עזרות might have to bring the calf. The גמרא suspects that ירושלים is excluded from this law altogether, and it will bring a source in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The calf whose neck is broken, brought for an unsolved murder
Subject to bringing, obligated to bring

phrases.aramaic: וִירוּשָׁלַיִם בַּת אֵתוֹיֵי עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה הִיא?
phrases.english: But is Jerusalem subject to bringing a heifer whose neck is broken?

steps.triggerLanguage: וִירוּשָׁלַיִם בַּת אֵתוֹיֵי עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption in רבי צדוק's question.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי צדוק's assumption that ירושלים might bring an עגלה ערופה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ירושלים may be excluded from the law of עגלה ערופה altogether.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists ten special laws of ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא listing ten unique laws of ירושלים. One of them exempts it from עגלה ערופה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: Ten things were said about ירושלים, and this is one of them:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces the source behind its challenge. It is setting up the quote, and the list continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says ירושלים has ten special laws that set it apart from other cities. The exemption from עגלה ערופה is one of them, and that contradicts רבי צדוק's question.

phrases.english: But was it not taught:
Ten things were said about Jerusalem,
and this is one of them:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the challenge in step 32.
steps.raayaObject: That ירושלים is exempt from עגלה ערופה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the ten special laws of ירושלים (quoted in the next part of the text).
